f_52176382.description: An exceptionally rare and highly sculptural early 20th-century Jugendstil and Arts & Crafts brass chandelier, dating to circa 1900–1915. Measuring an impressive 30.5 inches in overall diameter, the chandelier is dominated by a monumental pierced brass dome whose architectural silhouette strongly recalls an early deep-sea diver’s helmet. Despite its remarkable nautical appearance, the fixture was conceived and constructed as a chandelier and is not a converted diving helmet. The large domed body is formed in brass and decorated with a highly distinctive combination of pierced geometric openings and applied stylized botanical ornament. Six repeated vertical motifs terminate in abstracted leaf forms, while additional foliate metalwork connects the outer lighting arms around the broad lower collar. The design is unusually bold and architectural, combining the geometric discipline of Continental Jugendstil with the material-driven construction associated with the Arts & Crafts movement. A particularly striking feature is the deep red interior of the pierced dome. A seventh light is mounted centrally inside the body, illuminating the red interior and allowing a warm red-orange glow to emerge through the pierced openings when the chandelier is lit. Six additional lights are arranged symmetrically around the outside, creating an unusually dramatic combination of direct and atmospheric illumination. Each of the six outer brass shade holders retains its original three-screw glass mounting system. The lower rims are pierced at regular intervals with small, equally spaced holes originally intended for a suspended glass-bead or glass-fringe decoration, now absent. Decorative glass-bead fringes were widely employed in both Jugendstil and Arts & Crafts lighting during the early years of electric illumination. The six frosted and cut-glass shades currently fitted to the chandelier are later period-appropriate additions and are not represented as original to the fixture. Their elongated form and geometric cut decoration complement the chandelier particularly well while allowing its exceptional brass structure to remain visually dominant. The construction is substantial and beautifully revealing of its period manufacture. Inside the dome, individual curved brass supports radiate from the central assembly and are mechanically secured to the body using small brackets and traditional slotted screws. The chandelier further incorporates separately formed brass housings, applied decorative elements and an elaborate sculptural suspension fitting at the crown. The brass retains a highly attractive aged surface with rubbing, oxidation, scratches and variations in tone developed through more than a century of use. It has not been aggressively polished, preserving the depth and character of the historic metalwork. No maker’s mark has been identified. Extensive research has so far failed to reveal another identical example, making this an exceptionally unusual surviving piece of early 20th-century decorative lighting. Its extraordinary helmet-like silhouette gives the chandelier an almost Jules Verne or early industrial-futurist presence, while its detailing remains firmly rooted in the decorative vocabulary of Jugendstil and Arts & Crafts design. Its monumental scale, warm atmospheric light and extraordinary sculptural presence make it particularly well suited as a statement piece for a high-end restaurant, cocktail bar, boutique hotel, private club or other distinctive hospitality interior. Again great value for money. Also, because our sharp price includes perfect packing and even worldwide delivery from our store to your door in just 4 to 5 workdays. f_52130972.description: An extraordinary architectural chandelier in bronze, created as much as a sculpture as a source of light. Dating to around 1900, this monumental European chandelier is an exceptionally rare example of the Neo-Pompeian and Neo-Classical taste combined with a highly unusual Orientalist figural program. The entire composition is built almost like a small classical pavilion or temple. Four tall fluted columns support the richly modeled upper structure, while between them stand four sculptural male figures wearing turban-like headdresses. One of the figures is shown with his hands pressed together in a devotional or prayer-like pose. Around the figures rise beautifully modeled serpents, making the snake motif one of the defining elements of the entire design. That theme continues all the way to the ceiling. Even the original suspension chain is remarkable: rather than ordinary links, it consists of a succession of individually sculpted, interlocking serpents. A further double-serpent motif crowns the chandelier itself. The amount of sculptural detail is exceptional. Human masks and heads appear throughout the architecture, including at the capitals of the columns and beneath the individual light platforms. The large sweeping arms terminate in sculptural mask-form supports, while the upper body combines classical ornament, fluting, shell-like forms and strongly architectural detailing. Stylistically, the chandelier belongs to the late 19th- and early 20th-century European fascination with antiquity. Its architecture is strongly Neo-Pompeian and Neo-Grec in character, while the four central figures and extensive serpent imagery introduce a distinctly Orientalist element. Comparable monumental figural chandeliers were produced in Germany around 1900–1910, particularly within the tradition of large patinated bronze Figurenleuchter. We therefore believe this chandelier to be Continental European and most likely German, dating from circa 1900–1910. One original threaded metal component is stamped “GS”. We have not been able to identify these initials with certainty, so no specific maker attribution is made. What makes this chandelier particularly impressive is the sheer number of lights. It carries 24 candle lights arranged around the exterior, together with a 25th concealed light in the center behind the four figures. When illuminated, this central bulb softly lights the sculptural pavilion from within and brings the figures and serpents beautifully to life. The chandelier will come with 24 matching candle covers and will be professionally rewired for safe use in the United States with 24 American E12 candelabra sockets and one American E26 socket. It is suitable for LED bulbs and can be used with a compatible dimmer. Despite its enormous scale and visual impact, the design remains remarkably balanced. At approximately 81.6 lbs, this is a substantial architectural light fixture intended for an important interior, grand entrance hall, staircase, dining room or other space capable of carrying a truly sculptural work of lighting. f_52104772.description: Weighing an impressive 17.6 pounds, this substantial Italian bronze wall plaque was created in honor of Saint Francis of Paola, the patron saint of Italian seafarers. The saint appears in high relief at the center, surrounded by a rich arrangement of maritime imagery. Anchors, dolphins, a ship’s wheel, compass rose, steamships and rolling waves fill the composition, while a heavy chain forms the outer border. Above the figure is the inscription San Francesco da Paola – Patrono della Gente del Mare: Saint Francis of Paola, Patron Saint of Seafarers. Across the anchors below appears the Latin invocation Ad litus educ Patriae, meaning “Lead us safely to our native shore.” The word Charitas—the saint’s traditional motto—is inscribed beside his halo. Saint Francis was particularly revered among Italian sailors, fishermen and port workers. Plaques bearing his image and maritime invocation were displayed aboard numerous Italian merchant vessels during the mid-20th century. This example may originally have been made for a ship or maritime institution, although its precise provenance is not documented. The deep relief, warm bronze patina and almost sculptural weight give it a commanding presence. It would make an evocative addition to a coastal interior, yacht club, maritime collection or study. The plaque is in good and fully original condition, with normal surface wear, minor marks and naturally developed patination consistent with its age. The reverse shows areas of green oxidation. f_51565182.description: Long before electricity entered the home, this remarkable object was created to hold a flame. Originally made as an imposing ecclesiastical candlestick, this late 19th-century Gothic Revival bronze has since been sensitively converted into a table lamp, giving an extraordinary piece of religious decorative art an entirely new life. What makes this example particularly fascinating is the iconography around its sculptural base. Seated female figures hold shields inscribed FIDES, CARITAS and SPES — the Latin words for Faith, Charity and Hope, the three theological virtues at the very heart of Christian teaching. Each virtue is accompanied by its own emblem. Fides, or Faith, is represented by the chalice; Caritas, or Charity, by the radiant heart; while Spes, Hope, carries its own symbolic device. Rather than being applied as small decorative details, these figures form an integral part of the architecture of the lamp and turn its base into an almost miniature Gothic monument. The rest of the casting is every bit as intriguing. The tall central column has an all-over diapered surface reminiscent of medieval metalwork and architectural ornament, interrupted by a richly modeled circular knop. Below, scrolling foliage grows around the seated figures and merges into four fantastical supports with powerful animal-like feet. Seen from different angles, new details continually appear. Faces, folds of drapery, shields, foliage, textured surfaces and sculptural feet all catch the light differently, giving this lamp considerably more presence than its relatively compact footprint might suggest. There is also something wonderfully contemporary about using an object of this age in this way. With a simple shade it becomes a highly functional table lamp, yet beneath the shade remains a substantial piece of 19th-century bronze sculpture with symbolism and craftsmanship that modern lighting simply cannot reproduce. It would make a particularly striking lamp on a console, library table, sideboard or large bedside table, and it would work equally well in a Gothic Revival interior, an eclectic collection or as an unexpected historic accent in an otherwise contemporary room. The bronze has retained a beautiful warm aged surface with the minor marks, rubbing and variations in patina one would expect from a genuine antique of this age. These traces of use add depth and character rather than detracting from the appearance. Originally conceived as a candlestick, it was later professionally converted for electrical use. The conversion is discreet and leaves the historic bronze body visually intact. f_51518362.description: There are desk accessories, and then there are objects that seem to embody the very idea of the written word. This remarkable and unusually large writing stand centers on a beautifully modeled bronze figure of Johannes Gutenberg, seated in late-medieval dress with a large printed folio spread across his lap. His long beard, fur-trimmed cap and cloak belong to the traditional imagery through which the pioneering printer has been represented for centuries, while the divided printed sheet he studies is an unmistakable reference to the world-changing art with which his name became synonymous. The imagery is particularly appropriate. Gutenberg's celebrated Bible of circa 1455 was printed predominantly in two columns of forty-two lines, and the sculptor has given the sheet on his lap that same visual rhythm of two densely printed fields. Rather than presenting Gutenberg as a remote historical monument, he is shown here as a working man examining the result of his craft. The figure sits at the center of an exceptionally substantial oval writing stand carved from richly figured Nero Portoro, the celebrated Italian black stone from the Ligurian coast, prized for its dramatic gold and occasional white veining. Against this almost architectural black-and-gold ground, the warm brown patina of the bronze is particularly effective. To either side are substantial patinated bronze writing vessels. One retains its hinged architectural lid with pointed finial together with a removable clear glass ink liner; its companion is an open, metal-lined receptacle. A long recessed tray across the front provides a resting place for a dip pen. We believe this piece was made in Central Europe, most likely within the German or Austrian cultural sphere, around 1900–1910. Its date is especially intriguing. The year 1900 marked the widely celebrated 500th anniversary of Gutenberg's presumed birth, prompting major festivities, exhibitions, medals and commemorative works throughout the German-speaking world. Although no maker's mark has yet been identified and we therefore cannot connect this inkstand directly with those celebrations, its subject and period make that historical context particularly compelling. Stylistically, the stand occupies that fascinating moment between late nineteenth-century Historicism and the early Jugendstil period: Renaissance imagery is combined with a much cleaner, more architectural treatment of the marble base and bronze fittings. At approximately 22 inches wide, this is not a small collector's inkwell but a genuine sculptural desk centerpiece. It would be particularly striking in a library, study, publishing office or interior where books, history and craftsmanship matter. The piece remains in good and highly decorative period condition with the expected surface wear, patination and minor marks consistent with age and use. The Portoro shows small edge imperfections and a visible old hairline/crack restoration to one area of the outer rim, all shown clearly in our photographs. One removable glass ink liner is retained. The open companion receptacle is metal lined and is shown exactly as it is today. A rare combination of sculpture, natural stone and writing history, and above all a wonderfully evocative tribute to the man whose work fundamentally changed the way knowledge could travel through the world. If you like this antique stand as much as we do then you will, again, love our price. f_51517862.description: Amazing sculpture of Jesus. There are religious sculptures that are primarily devotional objects, and there are others whose artistic presence reaches far beyond their original purpose. This remarkable Art Deco bronze figure of Christ unquestionably belongs to the latter category. Created in Europe during the first half of the 20th century, most likely circa 1925-1930, this unusually stylized Corpus Christi is a particularly powerful example of the way Art Deco artists reinterpreted centuries-old imagery through an entirely modern visual language. Rather than striving for anatomical realism, the sculptor reduced the human form to a series of strong, almost architectural planes. The elongated arms, pronounced rib cage, angular abdomen and sharply folded loincloth give the figure an unmistakably sculptural rhythm. Particularly striking are the oversized hands and feet, deliberately emphasized and beautifully modeled. The face may be the strongest element of all. With its deeply cut features, long hair, beard and upward gaze, Christ is rendered with an intensity that changes dramatically when viewed from different angles. The crown of thorns has likewise been simplified into broad, almost geometric forms, perfectly in keeping with the Art Deco aesthetic. Nearly two thousand years after the life of Christ, the themes embodied by this sculpture remain remarkably relevant. History continues to remind us that speaking the truth, challenging injustice and standing up to those in power can come at an extraordinary personal cost. Seen in that light, this sculpture is not merely a representation of the Crucifixion, but also a timeless symbol of courage, conviction, sacrifice and the price that can accompany uncompromising truth. That deeper meaning gives this bronze a presence that reaches well beyond its decorative qualities. For a collector of religious art it can be profoundly devotional, while for others it may equally be appreciated as a powerful humanist work about integrity, suffering and moral courage. It would also make an exceptionally meaningful gift for a devout friend, family member or collector. What makes this piece even more unusual is its substantial construction. Weighing approximately 9 kilograms / 19.8 lbs, this is no lightweight decorative casting. In the hand it immediately communicates the quality and physical presence of a serious bronze sculpture. The dark, almost black-brown surface beautifully emphasizes the modeling, while subtle variations and traces of age reveal the bronze underneath and give the sculpture the depth that only an older piece can acquire. At just 18.8 inches high, the work has surprisingly monumental presence. It could make a dramatic focal point in an eclectic interior, against a limestone or plaster wall, among Old Master paintings, or equally successfully in an otherwise restrained contemporary setting. Removed from the context of a traditional wooden cross, its silhouette becomes particularly striking and almost architectural. For collectors of Art Deco sculpture, Modernist religious art or distinctive European bronzes, this is the kind of object that is becoming increasingly difficult to find: immediately recognizable in subject, yet anything but conventional in execution. The softly purple-tinted glass warms to shades of rose, amber and champagne, while the deeply rounded glass lobes refract the light outward and create spectacular flower-like patterns across the ceiling and surrounding walls. The result is almost architectural: a relatively compact pendant producing a surprisingly large and atmospheric play of light. What makes this fixture especially appealing is the contrast between the substantial, almost sculptural glass body and the delicate metal cage surrounding it. Slender ribs follow the contours of the glass, while small scrolls and hand-worked decorative details give the framework a wonderfully organic rhythm. Viewed from below, the pendant resembles an opening flower, with the glass sections arranged almost like overlapping petals around the central light source. The original-style suspension is equally charming. Long, irregularly shaped metal links lead upward to a beautifully formed leaf-shaped ceiling canopy, giving the complete fixture a distinctly handcrafted character that would be difficult to reproduce today. Its smoky amethyst coloration is particularly attractive in daylight. Depending on the surroundings, the glass can appear purple, aubergine, smoky brown or even soft rose. When illuminated, those cooler tones become warmer and more transparent, which makes this fixture especially suited to interiors where atmosphere matters as much as the object itself. We can imagine this pendant making a memorable statement in an entrance hall, powder room, bedroom, dressing room, reading corner or above a small dining table. It would work equally well as an unexpected jewel in a contemporary interior, where its sculptural shape and warm light could provide a wonderful counterpoint to cleaner modern lines. f_51449012.description: Rare late 19th century sculptural weather station with hand-carved dragon. Some antique objects are interesting because of what they were made to do. Others because of how they were made. This remarkable barometer and thermometer succeeds on both counts. Dating from the late 19th century, circa 1890-1900, this highly decorative wall-mounted weather station appears to have been made in France in the fashionable Japonisme or Chinoiserie taste, most likely specifically for the Dutch market. At the very top is its most striking feature: an exceptionally expressive hand-carved dragon. Its long, serpentine body twists around the upper section, with its claws, scales, open mouth, horns and curling tail all individually carved. It gives the entire piece an almost sculptural presence and makes this much more than simply an antique barometer. The remainder of the wooden surround is equally interesting. Open geometric fretwork, asymmetrical scrolling elements and delicately carved flowering branches create a distinctly East Asian-inspired composition. Rather than being applied decoration, these motifs form part of the architecture of the entire case, giving it a particularly successful and sophisticated Japonisme character. In the center is the original circular Metallic Barometer, with its mechanism still visible behind the dial. The scale is printed with wonderfully evocative Dutch weather descriptions including Storm, Regen, Veranderlijk, Mooi W., Bestendig and Zeer Droog. Adding another layer to its history, the original barometer dial is marked ‘De Gruyter’s Stores – Amsterdam’, indicating that this French Japonisme weather station was most likely produced specifically for the Dutch market.” Above the barometer is the original enamel thermometer with both Celsius and Fahrenheit scales, neatly incorporated into the carved wooden frame. The combination of French-inspired Japonisme carving, Dutch lettering, a dragon, flowering branches, scientific instruments and period retail provenance makes this an unusually complete object. It would be equally at home in a collection of antique scientific instruments, Japonisme and Chinoiserie works, Dutch decorative arts or simply as a highly individual piece of wall decoration. The wood has acquired a particularly attractive warm patina, with darker tones remaining in the deeper carved areas and softer highlights across the raised surfaces. This natural ageing enhances the depth of the carving beautifully. The barometer dial shows age-related discoloration and wear, particularly toward the lower edge, all consistent with its considerable age and clearly visible in our photographs. The wooden carving too shows minor traces of age and use. We have not professionally calibrated the barometer or thermometer and therefore sell the instruments primarily as antique decorative and historical objects. A rare survivor from an era when even something as practical as checking the weather could be housed in a work of craftsmanship. Our favourable price includes professional packing and complimentary worldwide delivery from our store to your door in just 4 to 5 business days. f_51346112.description: Striking mid-20th century hand-painted portrait of a Native American chief. Dating from circa 1940-1950, this atmospheric portrait was painted directly onto an old wooden panel and remains in its original, wonderfully simple oakwood frame. The unusual pointed upper section of both panel and frame gives the work an architectural quality and makes it particularly decorative when displayed on a wall. The chief is portrayed in profile wearing an elaborate feathered headdress, with long braided hair and a red neck garment. Rather than relying on fine academic detail, the unknown artist worked with broad, visible brushstrokes and a warm, earthy palette of ochre, brown, rust-red, black and muted cream. Particularly attractive is the loosely painted background, where the colors seem almost to dissolve into one another and give the portrait considerable depth and atmosphere. The painting has clearly lived a life. Small marks, variations, scratches and areas of wear remain visible throughout the painted surface, while the oak frame also shows age-related wear and patination. In our view, these imperfections are very much part of the appeal of this piece and give it the authentic appearance one hopes to find in an approximately 75-85 year old decorative painting. We have deliberately left it untouched rather than attempting to make it look newer than it is. The reverse is equally telling, with the aged plywood construction and numerous old fixing nails around the perimeter clearly visible. There is no visible artist's signature and we have not attributed the sitter to a particular historical person or Native American nation. It should therefore be regarded as a decorative mid-century interpretation of a Native American chief rather than a documented ethnographic portrait. A characterful and highly decorative period painting that would make a strong accent piece in a study, library, lodge-style interior, eclectic living space or collection of folk and Americana-inspired art. The sculptural bronze group is beautifully modelled and finely cast, with Saint Mark shown in a contemplative pose holding an open book inscribed “Parate Viam Domini”, “Prepare the way of the Lord.” The subject gives the clock a strong biblical and intellectual character, while the presence of the lion adds power and balance to the composition. Some antique objects immediately reveal how much attention once went into even the smallest pieces made for the home. This highly decorative French jewelry or trinket box is a fine example. Dating from circa 1900-1920, it combines richly worked gilt brass with unusually thick, beautifully cut and beveled glass. The shapely lid is particularly attractive. Rather than using a simple flat pane, the maker fitted a substantial glass panel with a broad, hand-cut beveled border. Set into its center is an ornate brass mount surrounding a classical female profile inscribed “AUTOMNE”, French for Autumn. This allegorical image of the season gives the box a wonderfully romantic and unmistakably French character. The brass body is equally decorative. Its sides are worked throughout with repeating floral ornaments, berries, rosettes and finely patterned latticework. These motifs, together with the softly curved outline of the box, show the influence of the Louis XVI tradition that remained so popular during the French Belle Époque. Opening the hinged lid reveals another delightful detail: the reverse of the central medallion is finished with its own small floral mount. Even areas that were normally hidden were given decorative attention, something that speaks to the quality and charm of the piece. f_47980402.description: Impressive and highly stylish early 20th-century carved wooden bear sculpture with brass bowl. This impressive and highly stylish early 20th-century carved wooden bear sculpture is a fine example of North-West European applied art, most likely originating from the Netherlands and dating to circa 1915–1930. The artist who hand-carved this wonderfully stylized seated bear has masterfully captured both strength and calm in its posture. Rather than striving for naturalistic detail, the sculptor chose to emphasize powerful simplified forms, allowing the mass of the animal to speak for itself. The deliberately visible chisel marks enhance the sculptural character and place this work firmly within the aesthetic of early Art Deco and Expressionist wood carving. The bear is seated in a contemplative pose and holds an original brass inset bowl, suggesting a functional purpose, possibly as an ashtray or small receptacle, yet the object clearly transcends pure utility. Like the best examples of applied Art from this period, function and sculpture are seamlessly united into a single, harmonious design. This sculpture is carved from solid hardwood and has developed a rich, warm patina over time. Subtle age-related wear and natural surface characteristics only add to its authenticity and visual appeal. The piece is unsigned, which is entirely consistent with high-quality atelier work from this era, particularly within the Haagse and Amsterdam wood-carving traditions. Works of this quality, originality, and sculptural presence are becoming increasingly difficult to find. This is not a mass-produced or tourist object, but a highly individual and expressive work, created by an accomplished and confident hand. A true conversation piece, it will look equally striking on a desk, side table, mantelpiece, or as part of a curated Art Deco or modernist interior. f_44735822.description: Meaningful and a monumental masterpiece: “La Vierge d'Albert” piece of the golden Virgin) by ), cast by Barbedienne, 1916. Step into the poetic depths of history with this extraordinary, large-scale gilt bronze sculpture titled "La Vierge d'Albert", an emotionally charged and symbolically rich work by Albert Dominique Roze (1861–1952), one of France’s most revered sculptors of the late 19th and early 20th century. Gracefully rendered and cast in 1916 by the prestigious F. Barbedienne Foundry, this sculpture is more than an artwork andit is a relic of resilience, faith, and the endurance of hope amidst the ravages of war. Over the past decade or two we have seen and sold many works of religious art, but we never before had the pleasure of offering such a unique bronze handcrafted piece. To have found a piece of this size, this great shape and in this beautiful condition more than made our day. The statue represents the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus aloft. It's known for its graceful and dynamic posture, symbolizing peace and protection. Historical & Artistic Significance: This luminous bronze, resting on an elegant rouge griotte marble base, depicts the Virgin Mary lifting the Christ Child heavenward, an image immortalized as "La Vierge Dorée d'Albert" and once crowning the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Brebières in Albert, France. The original was destroyed during the First World War, becoming a powerful symbol of both devastation and divine protection. Etched with the date 25 Mai 1916, this particular cast was created during the height of the war and a poignant echo of the original statue's collapse after months of relentless shelling. Roze’s signature ("ALB ROZE") and Barbedienne’s foundry mark ("F.B.") are both clearly inscribed, anchoring this piece firmly in the heritage of European monumental sculpture. La Vierge d'Albert" is not just a devotional image and it is a beacon of French wartime endurance, once believed to signify the fate of the war itself: legend said that when the statue fell, the war would end. In that symbolic descent, and in this glorious recreation, we find the eternal dance between loss and hope. This piece is ideal for the discerning collector of religious iconography, lovers of French historic art, or curators of emotionally powerful 20th-century bronzes. f_44636362.description: Incredible handcrafted and mouth-blown glass table fountain and light fixture. This rare Murano glass table fountain is a spectacular fusion of sculpture, light, and water — a true showpiece. Attributed to the studio of Gino Cenedese, one of the most celebrated Venetian glassmakers, it’s a masterwork of hand-blown artistry and gold-infused glass. At its center is a twisted emerald-glass column, supporting a poised female figure at the top, surrounded below by four playful male figures, each uniquely modeled. The composition may represent an allegory of music, nature, and celebration. The central female figure evokes a muse or goddess, while the surrounding male figures — two with musical instruments and two with flowers — suggest themes of joyful expression, beauty, and abundance. Together, they create a scene that feels both harmonious and timeless — a tribute to the pleasures of life, rendered entirely in glass. Between the four figures, large translucent blossoms bloom from the basin, each hiding a tiny fountain spout. When activated, water or champagne flows gently from the flowers, catching the light and shimmering as it cascades into the green marbled glass basin. The piece is richly accented with cordonato d’oro — an intricate Murano technique that incorporates 24k gold leaf directly into the glass. This gives the entire fountain a subtle golden glow, especially when illuminated. These fountains were rarely made and always one-of-a-kind — often commissioned for grand homes or luxury interiors. This example is not just decorative, but fully functional and electrified, with its fountain mechanism and interior light both in working condition. *Gino Cenedese (1907–1973) was one of the leading figures in Murano glassmaking during the 20th century. He founded his own glassworks, Gino Cenedese & C., in 1946, right after World War II — a time when Murano was beginning a creative revival. Cenedese collaborated with renowned designers and artists, including Fulvio Bianconi and Alfredo Barbini, and became known for combining classical techniques with bold, expressive forms. His studio was especially admired for its innovative use of color, gold leaf, and figurative elements, all of which are beautifully reflected in this fountain. Pieces attributed to Cenedese are highly collectible today and continue to represent the elegance, craftsmanship, and spirit of postwar Venetian design that made Murano world-famous. This extraordinary craftsmanship fountain/light therefor too is great value for money. But also, because perfect packing and worldwide shipping from our store to your door in just 2 to 5 workdays are complimentary as well. If you're in the U.S., you'll just need a simple step-up voltage converter (from 110V to 220V) to use it. These are easy to find online or at electronics shops. The difference in frequency (50Hz vs 60Hz) typically isn’t an issue for this kind of pump, but if you’re planning to use it regularly, it’s always a good idea to check with an electrician. *The twisted emerald glass column has a non-structural surface crack — it does not run through and the piece remains stable and visually striking. f_43696862.description: Another top quality, antique French pendant light with a perfect Art Deco design. This stunning and finer quality Art Deco ceiling lamp was realized by glass studio Léon Auguste Hugue (Paris, 1878 – Clichy-la-Garenne, 1970) who began his career as a bronze fitter. In 1907, he established his own bronze lighting manufacturing business at 14 rue Pierre Levée. In 1913, he created a new limited partnership, "L. Hugue, fabrique de bronzes et d’appareils d’éclairage," at number 10 in the same street. The business grew, and around 1925, he set up a factory at 68 rue des Rondeaux, where he worked with the help of his son Maurice Léon, also a bronze fitter. At the 1927 Exhibition in Madrid, he received the Gold Medal diploma alongside Francis Hubens. Strangely, in 1932, Léon Hugue sold his company to Charles Frères, only to re-purchase just the factory at 68 rue des Rondeaux two years later, in 1934. Following the death of his third wife, Marie-Félicie Foussard, in 1938 (he was married four times in total), Léon Hugue had to buy back her shares, which had been inherited by his granddaughter Claudine-Jeanne Ranc, also the granddaughter of another major bronze lighting manufacturer, Charles Ranc. His company remained active until at least the beginning of World War II. Léon Hugue passed away in Clichy-la-Garenne shortly before his 92nd birthday. The stylish shade -in frosted and molded glass- offers a wealth of geometric patterns in relief. This is a stunning example of Art Deco design by one of the great lighting studios of the period. Like all timeless designs, it would be a winning addition to any style of interior from classic Deco to contemporary. This good size and stylish Art Deco fixture from the heydays of the European Art Deco era will bring class, style and the most beautiful warm light in your living space. The geometric design of this superb shade is simply to die for and it comes with 'rope chain' which is simply perfect to connect the stunning shade and the striking and matching design, silvered bronze canopy with. The combination of the geometrical glass shade and the perfect bronze canopy is an absolute joy to look at. Both with the light switched on and off, this rare light fixture, signed by French craftsman Hugue, is a real eyecatcher that can be used in virtually every kind of room. Thanks to its timeless design and beauiful quality materials it brings class and beauty like no modern fixture ever could. f_40497992.description: Stunning religious wall panel in thick relief with strong hook for easy mounting. For the collectors of stunning antique church relics we are also offering this marvelously hand carved pelican sculpture for wall mounting. The character ascribed to the pelican in this context is nearly as fabulous as that of the phœnix. From a clumsy, gluttonous, piscivorous water-bird, it was by the growth of legends transformed into a mystic emblem of Christ, whom Dante terms "Nostro Pelicano". St. Hieronymus gives the story of the pelican restoring its young ones destroyed by serpents as an illustration of the destruction of man by the old Serpent, and his salvation by the blood of Christ. The pelican in Christian art is an emblem of Jesus Christ, by "whose blood we are healed" and it is also a symbol of charity. Many early painters and carvers mistakenly represented it more similar to an eagle (much like in this antique church relic), and not as a natural pelican which is why most people today still are a bit confused at first when this stunning hand carved, symbolic bird is called a pelican. This striking and all hand carved, symbolic panel was originally part of a church or monastery communion rail and it is a real work of (religious) art. Brom of Utrecht was a family (or dynasty) of goldsmiths in the Dutch city of Utrecht and they were known for creating some of the best ecclesiastical art that was available in the second half of the 19th and in the first half of the 20th century (from 1856 to 1961 to be exact). They were both designers and manufacturers and, as it goes with truly good makers, they also attracted the interest of other top designers from that era. Those other top designers needed a company to handcraft their top quality designs and Brom of Utrecht was one of the 'go-to' companies for many decades. Those designers were Steph Uiterwaal, Jos Pinker, Wilfried Put, Jo Uiterwaal and Maarten Zwollo. It will be very difficult to ever find a more beautifully designed and geometrically more pure and perfect, Art & Crafts cross and Christ sculpture. This large size, standing crucifix truly is a stunning and impressive work of religious art that will never fail to impress you or anyone visiting. This Christian work of art dates from the 1910s or 1920s and although over the centuries crucifixes have been made in all kinds of shapes and sizes, the ones from the Arts & Crafts era seem to be the most distinctive in style. And this pure Arts & Crafts crucifix certainly is no exception. The straight lined and geometrical details in this Jesus sculpture are among the best we have seen. f_36982542.description: One of a kind and all hand-crafted, good size antique box by Alfred Daguet (1875-1942). Alfred Daguet was a French craftsman/metalsmith, active around the early 1900s and who specialized in repoussé copper panels applied to hinged boxes, mantel clocks, and other exquisite objects. His atelier was above Siegfried Bing's famous showroom, Maison de l'Art Nouveau, that displayed his works as well as those by Louis Comfort Tiffany and numerous other Art Nouveau artists such as Clément Massier, Eugène Gaillard and Georges de Feure. Bing was a major proponent of the Art Nouveau movement and his pavilion at the Exposition Universelle of 1900 in Paris signified to the world the importance of this new style. So if you are looking for a truly stylish AND artistically decorative, antique box to grace your table, dresser or display cabinet then this Art Nouveau-gem could be yours to enjoy soon. The frame of this box is made of wood and the perfectly embossed 'skin' is all hand-crafted out of brass or patinated copper. Each side of this stunning box has its own beautiful decor and each has been hand-hammered onto the wooden frame with tiny brass nails. There is something about these organic patterns combined with the vibrant cobochon colors that appeals to collectors all over the world and it has made these antique boxes extra valuable. From start to finish, it must have taken weeks rather than days to first design (hand-draw) and then hand-create this truly unique box. Perfectly inlaid into the brass are some wonderful blue, green and red gemstones. The combination of the stunning color 'stones' and the various patterns in which they are placed, gives this antique box a truly artistic and also modernist look and feel. In a way Daguet, just like for example Antoni Gaudí, created his own type of Art Nouveau. This antique box also is in superb condition, it has a remarkable patina and it comes with a perfect working lock and key. No matter what you decide to use it for and no matter where you decide to have it on display, this antique box will never fail to impress. Our more than fair price for this beautiful Art Nouveau répoussé box even includes perfect packing and also free delivery from our store to your door in just 4 to 5 days. f_33653242.description: Beautiful large tile painting of a Gothic church interior by W.B. van Horssen (1863-1931). We very recently purchased a small collection of very rare antique plaques, tiles and vases by some of the best known maker's in the history of Dutch ceramics. This unique, hand-crafted and hand-painted work of art is the first one of that collection and this stunning and rare, single tiles plaque is in its original wooden frame. Because of their contrasting colors, the frame and tile painting go together really well. And these are in fact two works of art, because both the stunningly hand-painted tile and the wooden frame are as good as they come. With the borders of the frame coming as far outward as they do and the Gothic church interior that is drawing your attention deep into the back of the church, they really complement each other. However beautiful the frame is, this antique ofcourse is about the painting and this particular painting is by one of Rozenburg's finest (Wijnand Bastiaan van Horssen) who has perfectly managed to enhance the depth that is already in this composition, thus creating a visual effect that is an absolute joy to look at. By the way, the price that you see on the 'sticker' that the former owner put on the back after he had purchased this piece was put there in the 'old days' when we still had the Dutch guilder. The original painting of the Nieuwe Kerk in the Hague Holland (built in circa 1650) was by J. Bosboom. Besides one small old crack and a few minor imperfections to the frame, this unique and wonderful work of art is in very good condition still and may it grace the home or chapel of a Gothic style enthousiast soon. Mind you, because of their relative fragility very few of these amazing and high value works of art are still around. Rozenburg of the Hague, where this unique tile painting was created, was always one of the greats in Dutch ceramics and many of their works grace museums all over Europe. Rozenburg’s shareholders included the likes of the marine painter H.W. Mesdag (1831-1915) and the poet and literary critic Carel Vosmaer (1826-1888), and its tile painters numbered rising artists like Willem de Zwart (1862-1931) and W.B. van Horssen (1863-1931). Many of the handpainted scenes were devised by these master painters and their apprentices. Inspiration and expertise were derived from field trips, the Hague art academy or volumes of illustrations from all over the world. So if you can see the beauty and appreciate the rareness and quality like we do then this stunning antique could be gracing your home or house of prayer soon. f_33635892.description: Stunning French bronze tazza with wine & Bacchus theme, by Ferdinand LEVILLAIN (1837-1905). Every time we find an antique of this extraordinary quality and beauty we wonder what people are looking for in stores in this day and age. In terms of the design, the beauty, the amazing techniques and the materials that were used to create this table piece, nothing modern even comes close. Just imagine the amount of work, the incredible skill and the dedication it would have took to create this piece from the 'drawing board' all the way to the polishing of the bronze bowl. And as it goes with top quality made antiques, this tazza too has only grown more beautiful, because of the many decades in which the rich patina was built up. You could place some tangerines (preferably grapes) or some flower petals in the outer ring of the bowl, but this work of art will look simply amazing by itself also. It is the best tazza we have seen in a long time. The central medallion depicts the child Bacchus and his 'helper', the stunning satyr who, by squashing a grape bunch in his right fist, serves up the child its first glass of 'wine'. Both the standing and drinking child and the casually sitting satyr are of a beauty and style that only the greater artists are capable of creating. Above this endearing scene are the perfect grape leafs and underneath it reads JOVUGLOS (latin for 'the little ones') and this medaillon is clearly marked F. Levillain 1866. Even more clearly marked is the base and there is the name of probably the best bronze foundry of Paris in the mid to late 1800s. The worldfamous name of BARBEDIENNE (yet another highly gifted Ferdinand) always is a guarantee of the best quality workmanship that money can buy. Have you also noticed the stunning bust sculptures (of an older Bacchus) 'growing out' of the base. All together this piece is like a masterclass of what fine art was meant to be like, stunning and meaningful. Ferdinand LEVILLAIN follows the teachings of the sculptor JOUFFROY (1806-1882), before entering the Salon des Artistes Français. His work stands out at the 1867 Universal Exhibition, in Paris, for a neo Greek style bronze vase of his authorship. In 1871, LEVILLAIN reaches notoriety thanks to his association with the renowned bronze caster Ferdinand BARBEDIENNE. His works for BARBEDIENNE figure in the most relevant international museums such as the Victoria & Albert Museum in London and the Metropolitan Museum in New York, as well as other artworks at the British Museum in London or at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris. f_28377042.description: Wonderfully handcrafted antique table or desk lamp for a unique ambiance. If you are looking for a rare, beautiful design and top quality hand-crafted table lamp then this remarkable specimen could be ideal to grace your living space. The artisan metal worker who handcrafted this fine quality and detailed antique lamp truly did a great job. Mind you, every single bronze arm, pillar, faun, finial, guirlande etc first had to have been sculptured out of clay (or another material) before a mold could have been made and before the boiling bronze could have been cast. Especially the detailed fauns, the long 'legs' with hooves and the guirlandes would have been extremely time consuming and challenging to create. From all the handcrafted parts that, together, make this table lamp then molds would have to be made. All the molds must then be filled with, in this case, liquid bronze. After the hardening of the bronze and removal from the molds, all the surplus material from the castings must be removed and all pieces would have been either gilt or patinated. Finally all pieces must be fitted together and around the marble base through welding and by drilling screwthreads etc. I am sure you will understand why they don't make top quality workmanship table lamps like this anymore. It would cost a fortune. When looking at this work-of-art lamp with this knowledge in mind, it makes this antique even more impressive and interesting. Again great value for money. Also, because perfect packing and worldwide delivery from our store to your door in just 4 to 6 days are free. f_22461182.description: Rare matching set of three Venetian mouth-blown glass wall sconces, Italy, circa 1950–1970. It is the construction of these Italian wall lights that makes them so attractive. Rather than simply decorating a metal frame with pieces of glass, the maker has used hand-blown glass to form almost the entire visible silhouette of each sconce. The two gracefully curved arms are made of glass, as are the shaped candle cups, the central wall section and the large teardrop finial underneath. Running through this transparent structure are the brass fittings and electrical components, creating a wonderful combination of warm golden metal and subtly smoked amber glass. Depending on the surrounding light, the glass can appear almost clear in places and warmer honey or champagne-colored in others. This restrained coloring makes the sconces much easier to combine with an interior than darker amber glass lighting. Their design is an elegant Venetian interpretation of the traditional two-arm candle sconce. The flowing glass arms and elongated candle cups give them a light and almost weightless appearance, while the brass details provide just enough contrast and warmth. And then there is the fact that there are three. f_19442902.description: Stunning firescreen with a famous earth angle, two famous saint paintings and more. With meaningful 'religious art' from centuries-past being one of our specialities we were amazed, not only to find this rare and marvelous fire screen, but also because of its excellent condition. But then again, we think we see that more often, because true beauty, quality and meaningful antiques radiate something that was already there when it was created. This 'something' commands respect and this is why most people take very good care of very special pieces. Since much of what we know now about Christianity and about monastic life in its various 'forms' was given shape since the life of Christ, but possibly mostly so in Gothic / Medieval times, much of this is expressed in European Gothic Art of the past circa 8 centuries. This rare and beautiful fire screen from the early 1800s, which can also be used as a small room divider or a unique work of (decorative) art, is one of those unique Gothic antiques. The hand-carved knight sculptures are 'fun' and meaningful at the same time, because one of them looks a little desperate and the other looks more at piece and in prayer. The hand-carved winged angel in the middle/ on top seems to be overlooking this 'Gesamtkunstwerk'. What makes this antique really stand out and what also makes it complete are the three hand-painted panels inside this screen. Each of the figures portrayed here have dedicated their lifes to doing good, giving love and hope and thus healing people. In the centre is a glorious painting (in medieval style) of Earth Angel St. Raphael and the boy Tobias. The lady Saint on the right, we feel, is Elizabeth of Hungary (1207-1231) and the Saint on the left, we feel, is either Francis de Sales or Benedict of Nursia. We know too little to be sure, but we think the new owner and custodian will know. Below this description will be a short story of each of the figures portrayed in this screen. With so much beauty, quality and deeper meaning combined in this unique work of Gothic art, we feel, it will find a good home soon. If you feel (or know) this piece should be yours to own and enjoy then it could be flying your way soon. Mind you, our price for this once-in-a-lifetime-find even includes perfect packing and also worldwide shipping from our store to your door in just 4 days. Maximum height x width x depth (of the feet): 45.2 x 36.5 x 13.5 inches. We have a passion for the unique, for quality, for stylish yet practical and for craftsmanship of years gone by. Your purchases will be extremely well packaged and we look forward to serving you (again). You can shop all our 1000+ listings by pushing the button that reads 'View All From Seller'. As promised earlier, here are short descriptions of the figures portrayed in this unique screen: 1. St. Raphael is one of the 7 Archangels who stand before the throne of the Lord, and one of the only three mentioned by name in the Bible. He appears, by name, only in the Book of Tobit. Raphael's name means "God heals." This identity came about because of the biblical story that claims he "healed" the earth when it was defiled by the sins of the fallen angels in the apocryphal book of Enoch. Based on the story of St. Raphael and Tobias, St. Raphael has long been considered the patron saint of healers, travelers and fishermen. 2. Elizabeth of Hungary (1207-1231) was a princess of the Kingdom of Hungary and a greatly venerated Catholic saint who was an early member of the Third Order of St. Francis, by which she is honored as its patroness. Elizabeth was married at the age of 14, and widowed at 20. After her husband's death she sent her children away and regained her dowry, using the money to build a hospital where she herself served the sick. She became a symbol of Christian charity after her death at the age of 24 and was canonized on 25 May 1235. 3A. Benedict of Nursia (?480-543 AD) is a Christian saint venerated in the Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Oriental Orthodox Churches, the Anglican Communion and Old Catholic Churches and he is a patron saint of Europe. Benedict's main achievement, his "Rule of Saint Benedict", contains a set of rules for his monks to follow. Heavily influenced by the writings of John Cassian, it shows strong affinity with the Rule of the Master, but it also has a unique spirit of balance, moderation and reasonableness, which persuaded most Christian religious communities founded throughout the Middle Ages to adopt it. As a result, his Rule became one of the most influential religious rules in Western Christendom. For this reason, Giuseppe Carletti regarded Benedict as the founder of Western Christian monasticism. 3B. Francis de Sales (1567-1622) was a Bishop of Geneva and is honored as a saint in the Catholic Church. He became noted for his deep faith and his gentle approach to the religious divisions in his land resulting from the Protestant Reformation. He is known also for his writings on the topic of spiritual direction and spiritual formation, particularly the Introduction to the Devout Life and the Treatise on the Love of God.

f_14477522.description: For the collectors of rare, beautiful, meaningful and usable Gothic Revival antiques. Since we had never heard of this phrase, we searched the web and this is one of the explanations we found: This Latin expression is addressed to Mary, the mother of Jesus, and means: Show yourself to be our Mother. It is taken from the ancient hymn Ave Maris Stella (Hail, Star of the Sea). When Jesus was dying on the Cross, He said to His beloved disciple: Behold your Mother. This ancient Latin prayer expresses our desire to receive Mary as our spiritual Mother too. f_8721263.description: Rare bronze sculpture of a joyous boy from the early 1900s. The sculptor of this Fine work of art has managed to capture the pure innocence and joy of a young child. Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna on Laughing Boy — The representation of children belongs among the most charming motifs revived by Renaissance art under the influence of Hellenism. Like a number of similar statuettes of equally unaffected charm, this one is probably the portrait of a child conceived as the infant Jesus. Such statuettes were commissioned to be set up in private chapels. The Laughing Boy is considered to be the last work of Desiderio da Settignano, who died young in 1464. This antique work of art will bring joy and beauty to your life, because the joy it radiates also is a joy to look at. On the left side of the base the founders mark reads: Fonderie National Des Bronzes, Ancien Firme J. Petermann St.Gilles -Bruxelles. The Fonderie National de Bronzes (1870-1967) was a Belgian company specializing in bronze casting. The company worked for Belgian, French and Dutch sculptors, including Toon Dupuis, August Falise, Jef Lambeaux and Auguste Rodin. This fine bronze too looks so much better in real life than in a picture and it will also make a great gift for yourself or a loved one. f_7141473.description: Stunning Arts and Crafts cupboard by one of the greatest. This wonderful handcrafted, stained oak cabinet was probably designed by Leonard Francis Wyburd (1865-1958) as it exhibits several style elements that are typical for his designs for Liberty & Co in the late 19th century. We have no pictures in books or other evidence, but the pieces from his hand that can be found on the internet reveal style elements that are very similar and they were used by no one else. The design of this incredibly artistic piece shows both the influences of Medieval and Rural Britain. It were these early and amazing pieces of furniture from the Liberty Studio (headed by Wyburd) that made people across the continent speak of the 'Stile Liberty'. Designers like Wyburd and pieces of furniture like this amazing cabinet, influenced and shaped the entire development of the Jugendstil and Art Nouveau in Europe. That too makes this rare piece important for collectors and possibly for museums around the world. This cupboard is a work of art and it is an absolute joy to look at. It is all made of solid and stained oak and apart from the stunning and impressive overal design with the overhanging top with supporting beams, there are some key style elements that make this cabinet really stand out. First of all, there is the ever so true saying which is embossed in copper in beautiful Arts and Crafts letters which reads 'WELCOME IS THE BEST CHEER'. Secondly, there are the rare leather panels in the doors which come with (faded) images in slight reliëf. The one on the left is of a man in a hat and tights and he is playing a mandolin. The leather artwork on the right shows (what looks to be) a female wearing a skirt and she is holding a tray. We have not figured out (yet) what is on the tray. Thirdly, there is the stunning designed and executed, brass handle on the drawer. In our opinion this historically important piece can only go to a museum or a private collector who has the right, Arts and Crafts, home for it. It is very practical in size and it can be taken apart, because it is build up in 3 pieces. . .the 'roof', the middle section with the doors and the base with the drawer. It may be difficult to see in our pictures, but the open base (below the drawer) does have a closed back in the section just below the drawer. . .the sides below the drawer are all open. By the way, the ivorine label of Liberty of London is attached to the inside of the drawer. Furthermore, the inside of this cabinet is just as clean and beautiful as the outside and both the doors and the drawer still open and close perfectly. This cabinet can nowadays be used for all kinds of purposes and it will really make an impression. . .wherever it stands. Mind you, professional packaging and delivery from our store to your door in 4 days is free. Maximum height x width x depth: 74 x 51.5 x 21.5 inches.
